Patient Vignette: Mr. P.

Mr. P. is a 72-year-old, married, South Eastern Asian man who presents for therapy at the urging of his adult daughter. He is soft-spoken, with a gentle, deliberate way of moving, as if he is always trying not to take up too much space. He has worked as a nanny for the same family for the past eleven years, caring for two children now aged nine and twelve. He describes his work with a quiet pride, emphasizing the importance of routine, patience, and a calm voice. “Children need to feel safe,” he tells me, his eyes fixed on the floor. “They need to know no one will shout.”

The trauma he carries began thirty-four years ago, when he was 38. He had recently married a woman who was, by all accounts, charismatic and forceful. He was a quiet man, working as a tailor, and she was a successful businesswoman. He describes the first incident as “a misunderstanding.” She had accused him of looking at another woman in a market. When he tried to explain, she slapped him. He was stunned. He did not fight back. “I thought, she is stressed. She will apologize.” She did not.

Over the next four years, the physical abuse became a fixture of their marriage. It was not daily, but it was predictable in its unpredictability. He learned to read the tightening of her jaw, the slight narrowing of her eyes. When he saw these signs, he would try to become invisible—moving slowly, speaking in a whisper, staying out of her path. But it rarely worked. She would hit him with her open hand, sometimes her fist, often with a wooden spoon or a plastic hanger. He never raised a hand to her. He never called the police. “In my culture,” he explains, “a man does not admit his wife beats him. It is shame. You are not a man.”

He left the marriage after four years, but the shame did not leave. He did not tell his family the real reason for the divorce. He said they were “incompatible.” For decades, he carried the secret alone.

Now, at 72, the past is no longer staying in the past. He cannot sleep. He wakes at 3:00 AM most nights, drenched in sweat, his heart pounding. The dreams are not of the hitting itself, he says, but of the moments before—the silence in the room, the sound of her footsteps, the feeling of his own body shrinking. He has begun to experience these sensations during the day, too. When the children he cares for raise their voices in play, his hands begin to tremble. When the father of the house comes home and closes the front door a little too firmly, Mr. P. feels a cold wave of nausea, and he has to excuse himself to the bathroom. He has started to avoid the kitchen, where the wooden spoons are kept in a ceramic jar. He asked his employer to put them in a drawer, inventing a story about dust.

His wife of the past twenty years, a kind and patient woman, does not understand. She touches his shoulder to comfort him, and he flinches. She asks him what is wrong, and he cannot find the words. He feels a profound isolation, as if he is living in two separate timelines: one where he is a gentle grandfather who makes rice porridge for the children, and another where he is a young man learning to be afraid of a woman’s footsteps. He has stopped attending the weekly community gatherings at his temple, because the crowded room makes him feel trapped. He spends his days off sitting in the park, watching the birds, feeling a deep, bone-weary exhaustion that sleep does not touch. He tells me, “I am tired of being afraid. I am 72. I should be at peace.” But the fear has made a home in his body, and it has no intention of leaving.
